report.tagline: The most visited US home search site, which makes money by sending home buyers to real estate agents and by listing rentals and selling mortgages.
report.simpleSummary: Zillow is a free website and app where Americans look at homes for sale or rent, see photos, prices and the 'Zestimate', an automatic guess of what a home is worth. When you click 'contact agent' or ask for a tour, Zillow sends you to a local real estate agent, and that agent pays Zillow. Zillow also earns from landlords who list rentals and from its own home loans. From 2018 to 2021 it tried buying and flipping homes itself, called Zillow Offers, lost a lot of money and shut it down.

overview.whatItDoes: Zillow runs the biggest home search portal in the US, plus Trulia, StreetEasy and HotPads. Buyers and renters use it for free. Zillow makes money by selling leads to agents (Premier Agent), charging rental listings, and offering mortgages through Zillow Home Loans. Its strategy is the 'housing super app': one place to search, tour, finance and rent.
howItWorks: Listings flow in from local MLS databases and agents; Zillow shows them with photos, price history and Zestimates.
A buyer taps 'request a tour'; Zillow passes this lead, called a connection, to a partner agent in that area.
Agents pay either a fee upfront for leads or, under the Flex model, a referral fee of a share of their commission when the home sale closes.
Zillow Home Loans offers mortgages to these buyers, earning on each loan.
Landlords and property managers pay to list rentals; renters can apply and pay rent online.
overview.valueProposition: For buyers and renters: every home in one free place with a value estimate. For agents: a steady stream of motivated buyers ready to tour.

businessModel.summary: Zillow gives search away for free and makes money from the people who want to reach buyers and renters: agents, landlords and lenders. Agent leads (Residential) are the biggest source of money, rentals are growing fastest, and mortgages add more per buyer.

revenueStreams.detail: $419 million in Q3 2026, from agents paying for buyer connections.
$220 million in Q3 2026, from landlords and property managers listing rentals.
$70 million in Q3 2026, from Zillow Home Loans.
Showcase, Follow Up Boss and other agent tools.

businessModel.pricing: Free for buyers, sellers and renters. Agents pay for leads by market or, under Flex, pay a referral fee of a share of their commission at closing (often reported around 35% to 40%). Rental listing prices are set by property type and market and are not fully public.
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a $400,000 home sale where the buyer's agent earns a 2.5% commission, $10,000. Under Flex, the agent may pay Zillow about 35% to 40% of that, so roughly $3,500 to $4,000. Zillow pays nothing to buy that home. If Zillow also gives the mortgage, it earns extra on the loan. Compare that with Zillow Offers, where Zillow bought homes with its own money and lost tens of thousands of dollars per home when prices moved. The lesson: Zillow makes the most money selling attention and leads, not owning houses.

growth.moat: Zillow's moat is a network effect: buyers come because almost every listing is there, and agents pay because the buyers are there. With 77% of category visitors, a rival needs huge traffic to compete. The threat is listings being kept off Zillow, which is why it is fighting Compass over private listings.

competitors.name: Realtor.com
competitors.positioning: Listing portal backed by News Corp and the realtor association data feed.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Zillow has far more traffic and more products like loans and rentals.

competitors.name: Homes.com (CoStar)
competitors.positioning: Portal that promises 'your listing, your lead', sending leads to the listing agent.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Zillow charges buyer agents for leads; Homes.com charges listing agents for visibility. CoStar spends heavily on ads to catch up.

competitors.name: Redfin (Rocket)
competitors.positioning: Portal with its own salaried agents, now part of Rocket Companies.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Zillow partners with independent agents rather than employing them.

competitors.name: Compass
competitors.positioning: Large brokerage pushing private listings shown first to its own clients.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Compass wants listings to stay inside its network; Zillow wants all listings public, and the two are suing each other.

competitors.name: Apartments.com
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Main rival in rentals; Zillow is growing fast in multifamily listings.

pmLessons: Know where your edge is. Zillow was great at attention and data, but buying homes needed pricing accuracy it did not have, and Zillow Offers failed.
A free product can be a great business if the right side of the market pays.
Network effects can be broken by supply: if listings leave, buyers leave.
Charging the paying side too much creates rivals and lawsuits.

interviewQuestions.question: Why did Zillow Offers fail?
interviewQuestions.hint: Explain the model, then the risk: the Zestimate pricing error at scale, holding costs, a market shift in 2021, and capital needs. Contrast with the lead model.

interviewQuestions.question: Zillow traffic dropped 3%. How would you investigate?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split by channel (Google, app, direct), device, region. Check AI search impact and seasonality. Propose fixes per cause.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you improve the Zestimate?
interviewQuestions.hint: Define accuracy goal, users (owners vs buyers), new data sources, show confidence. Measure median error.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Zillow's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Transactions completed through Zillow. Break into shoppers, connections, close rate; add guardrails for buyer trust.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Zillow list private listings or fight them?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh buyer access, agent relationships, legal risk and the network effect. Suggest a policy and how to measure impact.
